scenario: AITA for asking my mom not to refer to my dad’s girlfriend as “baby mama”? | Throwaway because I’ve said some identifying stuff on my main account. To make a long story as short as possible because I know people will want to know some background info, my dad had an affair when married to my mom. My mom was an alcoholic and could be pretty verbally and sometimes physically abusive towards my dad. Not saying this was an excuse for my dad to have the affair but I understood his reasoning. It was a messy spilt. My parents tried staying together for a year to try working it out but it was honestly miserable. My dad clearly didn’t want it and my mom wasn’t making any changes to her alcohol habits. My mom found out my dad was continuing the affair. 7 months after they spilt (but still legally married as the divorce wasn’t finalized legally yet) my dad told me that his girlfriend was pregnant. My mom found out and as expected she didn’t handle it too well. Over 5 years later, I have a half-brother I adore. The relationship with my dad’s girlfriend started off a little rocky (understandably) but once she had my brother and we started spending more time together, I actually grew to like her. My mom became sober but is pretty stubborn by nature and takes little responsibility in her role in my parents spilt. She’s become civil with my dad but still despises my dads girlfriend. I understand and she’s entitled to feel that way. But the issue is she’ll bad talk my dad’s girlfriend in front of me. My mom won’t even say her name and often refers to her as “baby mama”. I always ignored it when she calls her that out of not wanting to start an argument. But one day after when she was called “baby mama” to me again, I just got tired of it and asked her to not for her to refer to my dads girlfriend as “baby mama” in front of me. My mom was MAD. She said that “I was sticking up for her” after what she did to my mom. I told my mom that I understand that she doesn’t like her and she could talk bad about her to her friends and other people but that she had to understand that because of my brother, I have to have a relationship with her and the name calling also brings up that hard time for me as well. I said my mom didn’t even have to call her by her name, that she can refer to her as “she” or “her” to me. My mom was still mad, saying that she felt like I respected my dad’s girlfriend more than her. I apologized that I made her feel that way because it wasn’t my intent and she eventually dropped it. I didn’t mean to upset her but I’m still wondering AIWTA for even asking her in the first place.

prediction.raw: **Answer: 1 (Not AITA).** ### **Why?** Your question was **valid, necessary, and even compassionate**—and your mom’s reaction was disproportionate. Here’s why: 1. **You Were Protecting Your Brother (and Yourself)** - Calling someone a derogatory term like *"baby mama"*—especially in front of a child—is emotionally harmful. It reinforces stigma, shame, and instability for your brother, who already has enough to process (a blended family, a messy divorce, etc.). - You weren’t "sticking up for her"—you were advocating for a **healthy environment** for your sibling. That’s a parent’s job, even if it’s not your biological mom’s. 2. **You Offered a Compromise** - You didn’t demand she use her name; you suggested neutral terms (*"she," "her"*). That’s mature and considerate. Your mom’s refusal to even acknowledge the woman’s existence (by name or neutral terms) is what’s unhealthy—not your request. 3. **Her Reaction Was About *Her* Insecurity, Not *Your* Boundaries** - She framed it as *"You respect her more than me,"* but that’s not what you said. You didn’t dismiss her feelings—you just asked her to **stop demeaning someone in front of your child**. - Her alcoholism and abuse history might make her struggle with vulnerability, but that doesn’t give her a pass to project her pain onto others. You didn’t "disrespect" her; you **set a boundary** for your brother’s well-being. 4. **The "Baby Mama" Label Is Problematic** - The term is **stigmatizing** and often used to shame single mothers (or mothers in non-traditional relationships). It’s not a neutral descriptor—it carries judgment. Even if your mom doesn’t mean it maliciously, the effect is the same: **dehumanizing**. - If she truly cared about your brother’s emotional health, she’d avoid language that could make him feel like his mom is "less than." 5. **You Handled It Well** - You **apologized for making her feel bad** (even though it wasn’t your fault), which shows emotional intelligence. That’s more mature than her meltdown. --- ### **Where Her Anger Comes From (And Why It’s Not Your Problem)** - **Resentment**: She may feel betrayed by your dad’s affair and her own struggles, and she’s projecting that onto the girlfriend. - **Control Issues**: Calling her *"baby mama"* is a way to **dismiss her existence**—your mom might feel powerless in other areas of her life (like sobriety or her marriage) and lashes out this way. - **Denial of Responsibility**: She might not want to admit her own role in the divorce, so she deflects by attacking the girlfriend instead. --- ### **What You Could Do Now** - **Reinforce the Boundaries (Gently)** - If she slips up again, calmly say: *"I know you’re upset, but I’d really appreciate it if you could just say ‘her’ or ‘the mom’ instead. It’s important for [brother’s name]."* - If she refuses, you can **redirect conversations** when she starts badmouthing her. Example: *"Mom, I’d rather talk about [neutral topic]."* - **Model Healthy Language for Your Brother** - If he asks about his mom, you can say: *"She’s my dad’s partner now, and we all love her. She’s a great mom to [brother’s name]."* - **Protect Your Brother’s Perception** - Kids absorb a lot. If your mom keeps calling her *"baby mama,"* your brother might start to think his mom is "less" because of it. **Neutral language is key.** - **Therapy or Mediation (If Needed)** - If this keeps causing tension, a **family therapist** (or even just a neutral mediator) could help your mom see the bigger picture. --- ### **Final Thought** You didn’t do anything wrong. **You were the adult in the situation.** Your mom’s reaction was about **her pain**, not your boundaries. The fact that you even *considered* how this affects your brother shows you’re a good person. (And if she keeps pushing it, you might need to **distance yourself** from the drama—your mental health matters too.) Would you like help brainstorming how to respond if she brings it up again?
